title: Impact of gonadotoxic therapies on fertility (FertiTOX). Distress factors of potential fertility impairments in oncology patients and resulting intrapersonal stress response – the significance of fertility preservation as a preventive measure
summary:
When someone is diagnosed with cancer, there are many things to consider. What is my prognosis and how will I feel during and after remission? Will I be unable to work? How will my appearance change? Will I be able to continue with my everyday life? What will my treatment and its side effects be like? How will those around me react and support me? One area that is unfortunately often neglected is fertility protection. Some people have a clear desire to have children at a young age, while others are still unsure in adulthood. This uncertainty is acceptable, as each person should actively decide for or against having children. In the case of cancer, certain forms of therapy can impair fertility, and this decision is taken out of a person's hands. The issue of fertility protection is therefore relevant for all cancer patients, regardless of their actual desire to have children, treatment and stage of disease.

This study aims to investigate where stress factors arise and in which individuals they can occur particularly frequently or intensely. In the long term, this should improve the care of cancer patients so that targeted support can be provided.
conditions: Follow-up examination after treatment for malignant neoplasms

interventions.name: Analysis of oncology patients with regard to various stress factors such as fertility distress, depression, coping, quality of life, fear of progression and others. criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
- Currently undergoing or having already completed potentially gonadotoxic therapy due to cancer
- Aged between 18 and 45
Exclusion criteria:
- no potentially gonadotoxic treatment, for instance due to benign tumour
